Hi Irene,

Thanks again for taking the time last week. We ran a short exercise with the site team to capture hard constraints for the on-prem Kubernetes cluster we want Redwood to run in our VPC. Two immediate items surfaced:

- Network: our primary datacenter only allows egress through an enforced proxy (explicit proxy auth) and a NAT/egress gateway on a small set of IPs. No direct outbound to arbitrary endpoints.
- Storage: we have existing SAN-backed block volumes with iSCSI connectivity. The storage team is wary of large ephemeral NVMe usage due to backup/replication processes.

Attached is a short PDF outlining the constraints and a diagram of the datacenter egress topology. Can you confirm whether Redwood’s agent/control-plane connectors can operate behind an explicit HTTP proxy (with basic auth) and whether the platform supports running predominantly on SAN blockstore (with small local NVMe cache only)?

Simon

Hi Simon — thanks for the diagram and the clear constraints. High level answers up front: yes, we can operate behind an explicit HTTP proxy and we can support SAN-backed block volumes as the primary PV class, with a small local NVMe cache for ephemeral working sets. There are trade-offs and a short list of follow-ups below.

Follow-ups / clarifying Qs:
1) Proxy auth: can you confirm the proxy supports basic auth or NTLM? We have a lightweight connector that supports basic auth with credential rotation — NTLM is more complex and we’d want to scope it.
2) Egress IPs: please provide the RFC1918-translation / NAT IP range that outbound traffic will be SNATed to — we need to whitelist on our control plane endpoints.
3) iSCSI details: what are typical IOPS and throughput per volume? Do you have limits on PV attachment counts per host?
4) Backups: your note about SAN replication — do snapshots run off-host (storage-initiated) or is the application expected to quiesce? This affects our recommended ephemeral vs persistent split.

Operational suggestions (quick):
- Node pools: recommend 3 node pools — control-plane (small VMs, dedicated), workers-gpu (if GPU required), and workers-cpu (standard inference). Because SAN is primary, put PVC-heavy services on the workers-cpu pool and reserve local NVMe for model cache on a dedicated cache DaemonSet.
- Storage classes: create a redwood-san sc (Retain|ReadWriteOnce) and a redwood-local-ssd sc (Ephemeral|ReadWriteOnce).
- KV cache: prefer being ephemeral and rebuilt from model store to avoid backup load.

I’ll loop Jonas for sizing recommendations and Marissa for runbook/on-call impacts. I’ve attached our standard preflight checklist spreadsheet — fill the yellow fields and return.

Best,
Irene Choi

Simon / Irene — quick sizing + technical notes from infra: 

Sizing (ballpark) for the initial pilot (single AZ rack):
- Control plane: 3x m5.large-equivalent VMs (2 vCPU / 8 GB) for the control agents and local control plane proxies.
- Workers-cpu: start with 6x c5.xlarge-equivalent (4 vCPU / 16 GB) if you intend to serve low-latency text generation RPS ~200 peak.
- Workers-gpu: if you need GPU inference, we recommend 2x A10 / A100-equivalent nodes to begin; we can tune batch sizes later.

Storage IO guidance:
- If SAN volumes are 10K IOPS aggregate but per-volume is limited to 2K, avoid placing many small PV-bound pods on a single host. Use topologySpread and PodAntiAffinity to distribute PVC consumers.
- For model cache: use ephemeral local NVMe of ~200–500 GB on each worker-gpu node, presented as a dedicated mount via DaemonSet; Redwood will manage eviction based on LRU. This keeps hot-model traffic off SAN.

Proxy and TLS notes:
- Our connector supports explicit HTTP proxies with Basic auth. For mTLS to Redwood control endpoints we prefer direct egress, but we can tunnel via the proxy if proxy allows CONNECT for TCP to port 443.

Action items for Simon: please paste the NAT egress IPs (one or more) and a sample SMART iSCSI perf report if available.

Thanks — Jonas
Infra Lead — Redwood Inference

Simon — operational checklist and a couple of gotchas from our onboarding experience:

- Backup interplay: if your SAN snapshots run at the array level and do not quiesce pods, we recommend using filesystem-safe snapshots (application-consistent where possible). Otherwise, mark model caches as excluded from snapshot policies.
- Monitoring: bring host-level metrics (iostat, tx/rx) into our console. If you cannot forward metrics out, we can run a short agent to push to a private S3-compatible bucket in your environment that our console polls (agent-to-s3 pattern).
- Upgrades: with SAN primary, cordon-and-drain times can be long if PVs reattach; we recommend shorter maxUnavailable thresholds on StatefulSets and staggered rolling updates.

Deliverables we’ll provide when you return the checklist:
1) A tailored node-pool YAML with resource requests/limits and topologySpread constraints.
2) StorageClass and PVC example manifests aligned to your iSCSI tuning.
3) Runbook entries for backup-exclusion, drain playbook, and incident steps.

I’ve attached a filled example of the preflight checklist for a sample customer to show the level of detail we need. Happy to run a 45-min preflight call next week to walk the site team through the yellow fields.

Cheers,
Marissa Cole
